item: Eight eMudhra G3B and G3C intermediates
claim: Eight eMudhra intermediates made at a 30 April 2025 key ceremony have P-384 private keys below 256, so anyone can recover the keys from the public certificates. Six are TLS CAs under emSign Root TLS CA - G3 and two are code-signing CAs under emSign Root CS CA - G3. The G3B CAs belong to eMudhra BV (Netherlands) and the G3C CAs to eMudhra Inc (US). They came from a batch of 24 intermediates generated that day, and only the P-384 keys of series B and C are affected.
note: Verified by inspecting the 16 certificates, 2026-10-31.

item: Sectigo cross-signs under AAA Certificate Services
claim: Sectigo cross-signed all eight intermediates under its AAA Certificate Services root, and each cross-sign reuses the same weak key, so 16 certificates are affected. eMudhra's eight are dated 30 April 2025 and expire on 28 April 2040. Sectigo's eight are dated 14 May 2025.
note: Verified by inspecting the 16 certificates, 2026-10-31.

claim: Each of the 16 certificates was matched to its serial, SHA-256 fingerprint and private key value. All 16 match the repo's rules/iocs.csv.
value: 16 certificates: 8 issued by eMudhra, 8 Sectigo cross-signs
note: Verified by inspecting the 16 certificates, 2026-10-31.

claim: Anyone holding one of the six TLS keys can issue a certificate for any website, and a client that still trusts the chain will accept it, which allows interception. The two code-signing keys could make malware appear to come from a trusted publisher on Windows.
Browsers trust the TLS intermediates through emSign ECC Root CA - G3, which cross-signs emSign Root TLS CA - G3. Mozilla, Chrome, Apple and Microsoft all trusted it.
note: Verified by inspecting the root certificate, 2026-10-31.

item: emSign Root TLS CA - G3 and emSign Root CS CA - G3
claim: The two G3 roots that issued the compromised intermediates were trusted as roots only by Microsoft.
note: Verified by inspecting the root certificates, 2026-10-31.

claim: AAA Certificate Services is a Sectigo root. Mozilla and Chrome had removed it before the incident, and Apple and Microsoft still trusted it.

eMudhra says its ceremony script generated each B and C series key and then, as a rehearsal, wrapped it, unwrapped it and imported it again, and the CA certificates were issued over the re-imported key objects. The affected keys were generated on Utimaco HSMs. Series A and A-1 were generated on Entrust nShield HSMs and did not go through the rehearsal.

item: Software with its own trust store
claim: The community tracker says its local Windows block applies only to clients that use the Windows certificate store, and that apps with their own CA bundle still need their own update. A Linux container trusts the CA bundle inside its image, so a patched host does not protect it.

Node.js bundles a snapshot of the Mozilla CA store fixed at release time, so only a Node.js upgrade changes it. Updating a JDK fixes only its bundled cacerts. Applications that ship their own JKS or PKCS12 truststore must have the roots removed from that file.

Removing only emSign ECC Root CA - G3 does not block the six Sectigo TLS cross-signs, because they chain to AAA Certificate Services. For macOS /etc/ssl/cert.pem, Apple's interim steps remove G3 and optionally AAA for this reason.
NSS and Firefox carry AAA Certificate Services trusted for email only. Mozilla did not add the Sectigo cross-signs to OneCRL, saying AAA Certificate Services is not in its root store.

claim: keytool -list -cacerts lists the JDK's bundled store and prints each entry's SHA-256 fingerprint by default, so a grep for the G3 and AAA fingerprints finds them under any alias. The store's initial password is changeit.
keytool -list -v prints each certificate's owner and issuer, so a grep on the Owner line matches the root by subject name.
A JDK's bundled store is lib/security/cacerts under the JDK home on JDK 11 and later, and jre/lib/security/cacerts on JDK 8.

For a runtime that can't be updated, OpenJDK says to back up cacerts, delete the four [jdk] aliases with keytool -delete and restart running Java processes. It says to ignore errors that a certificate does not exist, because not every runtime has all four.

As a last resort for TLS clients, OpenJDK suggests turning on revocation checking with -Dcom.sun.net.ssl.checkRevocation=true and -Dcom.sun.security.enableCRLDP=true. For signed JARs on JDK 17 and later it suggests jarsigner -verify -revcheck -strict.

OpenJDK's CheckCerts.java prints BAD ROOT for any trusted root whose subject names G3, AAA, G1 or G2, and exits with status 1. Its own comments class G1 and G2 as unrelated to the compromised intermediates.
Each Java installation has its own cacerts, so a machine with several JDKs needs each one checked and fixed. A running Java process keeps the store it loaded until it restarts.

claim: On Debian, Ubuntu and derivatives, updating ca-certificates and ca-certificates-java does not refresh /etc/ssl/certs/java/cacerts, because of a long-standing ca-certificates-java bug.
OpenJDK's Debian workaround is to delete /etc/ssl/certs/java/cacerts as root and rebuild it with update-ca-certificates --fresh.
IBM's keytool commands remove the root only from the runtime's default cacerts. IBM says applications with their own JKS or PKCS12 truststore must have the roots removed from that file.
A JDK keeps its cacerts in lib/security under the Java home from JDK 9 on. In JDK 8 it is in the JRE's lib/security, which is jre/lib/security inside a JDK.

claim: A password-encrypted PKCS #12 entry is a PKCS #7 EncryptedData with OID 1.2.840.113549.1.7.6. The JDK's own cacerts has been a password-less PKCS #12 since JDK-8275252, so its certificates stay readable.

Its PKCS12 probe accepts a PFX that opens with a SEQUENCE of any length form, BER indefinite (30 80), short or one to four length bytes, then version 3 (02 01 03) and an authSafe ContentInfo of type data (OID 1.2.840.113549.1.7.1). RFC 7292 allows BER for the PFX.
value: JKS FEEDFEED, JCEKS CECECECE, PKCS12 30 80 or 30 xx to 30 84, 02 01 03, data OID

claim: Every certifi release from 2019.3.9 through 2026.7.22 bundles emSign ECC Root CA - G3. Each bundle names the root in a Label comment, so it can be found by name as well as by fingerprint.
note: Verified by inspecting the package, 2026-10-31.

claim: certifi 2026.10.18, published 2026-10-18, removed all four emSign roots: the compromised G3 and the unaffected G1, C1 and C3. Users reported that it broke connections to sites that chain to the other emSign roots.
note: Verified by inspecting the package, 2026-10-31. The breakage reports are user comments on the certifi issue.

claim: GHSA-6q48-6c7w-9gw2 lists certifi from 2019.03.09 up to 2026.10.18 as vulnerable, with 2026.10.18 as the first patched release. certifi 2026.10.19 restores emSign Root CA - G1, C1 and C3 and still leaves out G3, and the PSF recommends it or later over 2026.10.18. It reached PyPI on 2026-10-20 despite its version number.
note: Verified by inspecting the package, 2026-10-31. GHSA-6q48-6c7w-9gw2 lists 2026.10.18 as the first patched release and itself advises 2026.10.19 or later. The PSF advisory recommends 2026.10.19 because 2026.10.18 also removed unaffected emSign roots. Neither release holds the G3 root.

claim: certifi 2026.10.23 keeps emSign Root CA - G1 as its only emSign root.
note: Verified by inspecting the package, 2026-10-31.

claim: Every certifi release up to and including 2025.1.31 also holds Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services root, which issued cross-signed copies of all eight compromised intermediates. That includes 2018.11.29, which has no G3 root and falls outside the GHSA range. Releases from 2025.4.26 on do not hold it.
note: Verified by inspecting the package, 2026-10-31. Disputed. GHSA-6q48-6c7w-9gw2 starts the vulnerable range at 2019.03.09 and covers only the G3 root. Inspection of the certifi wheels finds the AAA root in every release up to 2025.1.31, including 2018.11.29, and the PSF thread says old certifi bundles hold it. That an old client builds a chain through the cross-sign is reasoning and was not tested live.

claim: python -m certifi prints the path of the bundle certifi uses. An installed certifi records its version in a certifi-VERSION.dist-info directory next to the certifi package in site-packages.
note: Verified by inspecting the package, 2026-10-31.

claim: A certifi pin appears as a requirement line such as certifi==2026.7.22 in requirements.txt, as a [[package]] entry with name = "certifi" followed by its version in poetry.lock and uv.lock, and under a "certifi" key with a "version": "==VERSION" field in Pipfile.lock.

pip carries its own copy of certifi at pip/_vendor/certifi/cacert.pem, separate from any installed certifi package. python -m pip debug prints that bundle's path and the vendored certifi version. pip 26.2.2 also names its certifi version in pip/_vendor/bom.cdx.json.
note: Verified by inspecting the package, 2026-10-31. The pip debug output format is provisional and may change.

claim: pip 26.2.2, released 2026-10-20, is the first pip whose vendored certifi (2026.10.19) leaves out emSign ECC Root CA - G3. pip 26.2.1 vendors certifi 2026.6.17, which holds G3. pip 24.0 and 25.0.1 vendor certifi 2023.7.22 and 2024.8.30, which hold both G3 and the AAA root.
note: Verified by inspecting the package, 2026-10-31.

claim: From pip 24.2, on Python 3.10 and later, pip trusts the system store and its vendored certifi together. Older pip uses only its vendored certifi. Either way, a fixed OS store does not stop pip before 26.2.2 trusting G3. REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE and --cert add CAs to pip's set and leave the vendored roots in place.
note: The point about REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE and --cert comes from a reply on the PSF forum thread (secondary). pip's own documentation on it was not read.

claim: Debian patches its pip package so the vendored certifi returns /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt. Debian's pip therefore follows the system ca-certificates package.
Every virtual environment has its own pip, so each existing venv needs pip upgraded on its own. A venv has a pyvenv.cfg file at its root.

uv verifies TLS by default against roots compiled into its binary. Up to 0.10.x it uses the webpki-roots crate, which stores each root as a subject name and public key, and from 0.11.0 the webpki-root-certs crate of full certificates. Releases before 0.13.4 include emSign ECC Root CA - G3. uv 0.13.4, released 2026-10-20, moves to webpki-root-certs 1.0.10, and its binary no longer holds the root.
note: Verified by inspecting the binary, 2026-10-31. The binary grep was confirmed on Linux x86_64 builds only. The crate each release locks was read from its pinned Cargo.lock, 2026-11-04.

claim: uv 0.13.5, released 2026-10-21, also rejects certificate chains that contain the compromised keys, through rustls-webpki 0.103.16.

uv 0.13.5 moves its managed CPython 3.11 and newer builds to versions that bundle pip 26.2.2. The new builds arrive only after uv python upgrade, and venvs pinned to an older patch version keep the old interpreter.

uv uses the operating system's verifier instead of its bundled roots when given --system-certs, UV_SYSTEM_CERTS=true or system-certs = true in uv.toml. Setting SSL_CERT_FILE or SSL_CERT_DIR replaces uv's default certificate source entirely, so uv then trusts only those certificates.
Python 3.15.1, 3.14.9 and 3.13.17 bundle pip 26.2.2 with certifi 2026.10.19.

Python 3.15.2, 3.14.10, 3.13.18, 3.12.16 and 3.11.18 make the ssl module reject chains that use the compromised intermediate keys (CVE-2026-115557). The check matches the public key, so it also rejects the Sectigo cross-signs, and it does not run when verification is off (CERT_NONE). 3.15.2 and 3.14.10 have binary installers, and 3.13.18, 3.12.16 and 3.11.18 are source-only releases.
The current Python 3.11 and 3.12 releases bundle pip 24.0 and 25.0.1. A reply on the PSF thread says security releases will not upgrade that pip. Both pip versions hold G3 and the AAA root.
note: Verified by inspecting the package, 2026-10-31. The statement that 3.11 and 3.12 security releases will not upgrade pip is a reply on the PSF forum thread (secondary).

claim: Python 3.10 and older are end of life and get no fix. uv's changelog says the pip bundled with CPython 3.9 and 3.10 still trusts emSign ECC Root CA - G3.
The python.org macOS installer includes the certifi bundle, which needs its own pip install --upgrade certifi run with that interpreter.
Requests takes its trusted CAs from the installed certifi package unless REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE or CURL_CA_BUNDLE points elsewhere, so updating certifi fixes it.
HTTPX verifies against the certifi bundle by default, so updating certifi fixes it.
truststore verifies against the operating system's certificate store instead of certifi, so it follows the OS store.

conda 26.9.4 requires certifi 2026.10.19 or later and ca-certificates 2026.10.20 or later on Anaconda main, or 2026.10.19 or later on conda-forge. The ca-certificates bundle is ssl/cacert.pem under the base directory on macOS and Linux, and Library/ssl/cacert.pem on Windows.
Each conda environment has its own certifi and ca-certificates, and updating base does not update the other environments.
conda-forge rebuilt mamba and libmamba with the CA minimum without changing the version number, so the build string has to be checked as well as the version.
Anaconda's main channel has not rebuilt its CA packages for osx-64, linux-ppc64le and linux-s390x, which it no longer supports.
Standalone Pixi binaries bundle their own roots. Pixi 0.82.1 fixes them with webpki-root-certs 1.0.10 and rustls-webpki 0.103.16.
The PSF advisory also lists sigstore 4.5.1 and virtualenv 21.14.12 as minimum versions.
note: Their release notes were not read, so the reason for each minimum is unconfirmed.

claim: Node.js compiles in a snapshot of the Mozilla CA store, fixed at release time and exposed as tls.rootCertificates. Only a Node.js upgrade changes it.
Node.js PR #66877 moved the bundled store to NSS 3.131.1, which removes emSign ECC Root CA - G3, emSign Root CA - C1 and emSign ECC Root CA - C3.
Node.js 22.23.4, released 2026-10-21 per its changelog, is the first 22.x release without emSign ECC Root CA - G3. The 22.23.3 binary still holds the root as PEM text.
note: Verified by inspecting the binary, 2026-10-31. Disputed. The Node.js 22 changelog dates 22.23.4 to 2026-10-21. The distribution index lists it as 2026-10-20. The binary grep was confirmed on Linux x64 builds only.

claim: The Node.js October 2026 security release lists the eMudhra CA update as a dependency change for 26.x, 24.x and 22.x, with no CVE.

NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS only adds certificates to the bundled roots, so it cannot remove emSign ECC Root CA - G3. --use-system-ca and NODE_USE_SYSTEM_CA=1 add the system store alongside the bundled roots, and Node.js does not apply the system's distrust settings.

--use-openssl-ca makes Node.js use OpenSSL's default CA store instead of its bundled one. On most Linux distributions the distribution maintains that store, and its location depends on how OpenSSL was configured.
note: Not tested against a fixed distribution store.

claim: The GitHub Advisory Database has no reviewed npm advisory for a package that vendors a CA bundle with the G3 root. Electron's is the only npm advisory about this incident from 2026-10-17 to 2026-10-31.

claim: Deno uses its bundled Mozilla roots by default. DENO_TLS_CA_STORE selects system, mozilla or both, in the order given.

Deno 2.9.8, released 2026-10-21, is the first Deno release without emSign ECC Root CA - G3. It moves to webpki-roots and webpki-root-certs 1.0.10 and to rustls-webpki 0.103.16, which rejects paths containing the eight compromised keys, cross-signs included. Deno 2.9.7 still holds G3.
note: Verified by inspecting the binary, 2026-10-31. Disputed. Deno issue #37056 reported that 2.9.8 was tagged with no release. The v2.9.8 release was published about an hour after the issue was filed, and the issue was closed as premature. A YARA hit for the compromised intermediates inside Deno 2.9.8 or later likely comes from its distrust list. Judge Deno by version and the root grep.

claim: The Deno 2.9.7 binary also holds Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services root. Its Cargo.lock pins webpki-root-certs 0.26.6 and webpki-roots 0.26.1. Deno 2.9.8 does not hold the root.
note: Verified by inspecting the binary, 2026-10-31. Which Deno code path loads the AAA root was not traced.

claim: CVE-2026-111943 (GO-2026-6809) covers only Go's standard library. Go added a denylist to crypto/x509 so that Certificate.Verify rejects the compromised intermediates.

claim: Go 1.26.10 and 1.27.3, released 2026-10-19, carry the denylist. Earlier releases, including 1.27.0 to 1.27.2, do not.

Go's fix matches the SHA-256 hashes of the eight intermediates' public keys (SPKI). Sectigo's cross-signs reuse those keys, so the denylist also rejects chains through AAA Certificate Services. It applies when Go hands verification to the macOS or Windows platform verifier too.
sources: S73 | title: [release-branch.go1.27] crypto/x509: distrust a handful of intermediates
note: Verified by inspecting the certificates, 2026-10-31.

claim: Go's standard library ships no root bundle. On Linux it reads the first system bundle it finds, starting with /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt, and SSL_CERT_FILE or SSL_CERT_DIR override that. From Go 1.27, setting either on macOS or Windows also turns off the platform verifier.
govulncheck -mode binary checks a compiled Go binary against the Go vulnerability database, which flags toolchains without the CVE-2026-111943 fix.

Importing golang.org/x/crypto/x509roots/fallback embeds a root set in the binary. The module has no tagged releases, so projects pin it by pseudo-version. Go uses those roots only when no custom roots, platform verifier or system pool is available, such as in a container with no CA bundle, or when GODEBUG=x509usefallbackroots=1 forces them.

The fallback bundle at v0.0.0-20260916154351-b853e4b620cd holds the G3 root. The 2026-10-20 update, v0.0.0-20261020153306-9f2b28d4331a, removes it along with emSign Root CA - C1 and emSign ECC Root CA - C3.
note: Verified by inspecting the package, 2026-10-31.

claim: The February 2025 fallback bundle, v0.0.0-20250203165127-fa5273e46196, and every earlier bundle back to the module's first commit also hold the AAA root. The May 2025 update, v0.0.0-20250512154111-9f6bf8449a9f, dropped AAA and kept G3.
note: Verified by inspecting the February and May 2025 module zips, and bundle.go at golang/crypto commits d0b316056be8, 152cdb1503eb and 8c4e668694cc by subject name, 2026-10-31.

claim: The Go vulnerability database has no advisory for golang.org/x/crypto/x509roots/fallback (searched 2026-10-31).

go version -m lists the fallback module and its pseudo-version in a binary that embeds it. A binary built with the old bundle contains the G3 root's subject, DER and SHA-256 as text. One built with the fixed bundle contains none of them.
note: Verified by inspecting the binary, 2026-10-31.

claim: webpki-roots compiles Mozilla's root set into the crate, so its roots change only when the crate is updated and the program is rebuilt.
RUSTSEC-2026-0381 marks webpki-roots releases that include the G3 root as affected. 1.0.10, published 2026-10-19, is the first fixed release, and 0.26.11 is listed as unaffected.

webpki-roots 1.0.9 holds the G3 root and 1.0.10 does not. 1.0.10 still holds emSign Root CA - C1 and emSign ECC Root CA - C3, which 1.0.11 (2026-10-23) removes in a separate change tracked in Mozilla Bug 2083709.
note: Verified by inspecting the package, 2026-10-31.

claim: webpki-roots 0.26.11 has no root list of its own. It re-exports its webpki-roots 1.x dependency, so it is safe only when Cargo.lock resolves that dependency to 1.0.10 or later. 0.26.10 and earlier carry their own list with the G3 root, and the 0.26 line has no other fix.
note: Verified by inspecting the package, 2026-10-31.

claim: webpki-roots 0.26.9 and earlier, including 0.25.4, also hold the AAA root. 0.26.10 dropped it.
note: Verified by inspecting the package, 2026-10-31.

claim: RUSTSEC-2026-0383 fixes webpki-root-certs in 1.0.10, and its 0.26.11 is a wrapper that needs a 1.x dependency of 1.0.10 or later. 1.0.9 holds the G3 root as a full certificate and 1.0.10 does not.
note: Verified by inspecting the package, 2026-10-31.

claim: webpki-root-certs 0.26.9 and earlier also hold the AAA root. 0.26.10 does not.

claim: The amazonlinux:2023 image has ca-certificates 2025.2.76-1.0.amzn2023.0.3 with the G3 root, and a plain dnf update leaves it there. The fix needs a newer release version, 0.4 with --releasever 2023.12.20261026 or 0.5 with --releasever=latest. Amazon Linux 2 is fixed in 2025.2.76-1.amzn2.0.3, and the amazonlinux:2 image checked had 0.2. The later builds of 26 October also drop AAA Certificate Services, which Amazon says has been untrusted for TLS since 2025.
